hops.title: Blind cavefish build eyes and then lose them
hops.text: Adult Mexican cavefish (*Astyanax mexicanus*) have no visible eyes, only skin where the eyes should be. Look at the adult alone and you would conclude the cave form never builds them. The embryos say otherwise. A cavefish embryo starts an eye with a lens and a layered retina. Then the lens dies by apoptosis, retinal cells follow, and the eye stops growing and degenerates. When William Jeffery's group transplanted a lens from the eyed, surface-dwelling form of the same species into a cavefish embryo's optic cup, fewer retinal cells died, and the retina kept growing. How fast the retinal cells divided did not change.

sources.citation: Yamamoto Y, Jeffery WR (2000). Central role for the lens in cave fish eye degeneration. Science 289(5479):631-633.
Strickler AG, Yamamoto Y, Jeffery WR (2007). The lens controls cell survival in the retina: evidence from the blind cavefish Astyanax. Developmental Biology 311(2):512-523.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pale eyeless cavefish swimming beside a silvery eyed fish of the same species in a dimly lit cave pool.
image.caption: Cavefish embryos start eyes, then lose them to cell death; the eyeless adult hides that history.

hops.title: Apoptosis was named for falling leaves, with a silent p
hops.text: Before 1972, the pathologist John Kerr called this kind of death "shrinkage necrosis." But it often appeared spontaneously, or as a normal response to the body's own signals, not only after injury, so Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie wanted a better word. Their 1972 paper thanks James Cormack, a professor of Greek at the University of Aberdeen, for suggesting *apoptosis*, a Greek word for petals dropping from flowers or leaves falling from trees. A footnote proposes how to say it: stress on the second-to-last syllable, and the second half pronounced like *ptosis*, a drooping upper eyelid, with the p silent. The two words share a root meaning "to fall."

sources.citation: Kerr JFR, Wyllie AH, Currie AR (1972). Apoptosis: a basic biological phenomenon with wide-ranging implications in tissue kinetics. British Journal of Cancer 26(4):239-257, footnote p. 241.
Galluzzi L, Vitale I et al. (2018). Molecular mechanisms of cell death: recommendations of the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death 2018. Cell Death & Differentiation.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage brass microscope on a wooden desk beside a stone window, with golden autumn leaves falling outside.
image.caption: Apoptosis is Greek for "falling off," as leaves fall from trees: fitting for a death that is often normal.

hops.title: Your fingers, duck feet and bat wings
hops.text: Spread your fingers and look at the skin between them. In the human embryo, the tissue between the future fingers dies by apoptosis as the digits separate, with macrophages gathered around the dying cells. How much of that tissue dies depends on the animal. In chicks and mice, signalling proteins called BMPs trigger the death and free the digits. Duck embryos make Gremlin, a BMP blocker, in the webs between their toes, and keep webbed feet. In the fruit bat *Carollia perspicillata*, apoptosis occurs between digits in both forelimbs and hindlimbs: its hind toes separate, while tissue between its long front fingers persists as part of the wing membrane.

sources.citation: Bečić T et al. (2016). Spatiotemporal distribution of proliferation, proapoptotic and antiapoptotic factors in the early human limb development. Acta Histochemica 118(5):527-536.
Merino R et al. (1999). The BMP antagonist Gremlin regulates outgrowth, chondrogenesis and programmed cell death in the developing limb. Development 126(23):5515-5522.

Weatherbee SD, Behringer RR, Rasweiler JJ 4th, Niswander LA (2006). Interdigital webbing retention in bat wings illustrates genetic changes underlying amniote limb diversification. PNAS 103(41):15103-15107.
Schindler M et al. (2025). Comparative single-cell analyses reveal evolutionary repurposing of a conserved gene programme in bat wing development. Nature Ecology & Evolution.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An open human hand with fingers spread, near a duck showing a webbed foot and a small bat with a webbed wing and separate hind toes.
image.caption: Embryos clear or keep tissue between digits: freed fingers in us, webbed feet in ducks, webbed wings in bats.
